items.content_html:
TL;DR: Vodafone sold a 5% effective stake in Safaricom to its own subsidiary, Vodacom, for Sh68 billion. Because Vodafone controls Vodacom, the money effectively returned to Vodafone—meaning the parent company funded its own exit from that slice of the business. The Kenyan government, by contrast, received genuine external cash of Sh204 billion for its 15% stake.

The recent restructuring of Safaricom's ownership has raised eyebrows for a simple reason: Vodafone essentially used its own money to fund the purchase of its additional stake in East Africa's most profitable company. At the heart of the transaction is a Sh68 billion payment that Vodafone received from its African subsidiary, Vodacom, for transferring a 5% effective interest in Safaricom. In plain terms, Vodafone sold a slice of Safaricom to Vodacom, and the Sh68 billion price tag flowed back to the parent company.

The Intra-Group Transaction Explained

To understand how this works, it helps to look at the broader deal. Vodacom agreed to acquire an additional 20% of Safaricom, lifting its total shareholding to 55%. The breakdown was as follows:

  • 15% from the Kenyan government at a cost of Sh204 billion
  • 5% from Vodafone for Sh68 billion

Since Vodafone is the ultimate parent of Vodacom, the Sh68 billion that Vodacom paid for the 5% stake effectively returned to Vodafone's own coffers. In other words, Vodafone did not need to bring in fresh external capital to exit that portion of its Safaricom holding; the money circulated within the group.

Why Vodafone's Sh68 Billion Never Left the Family

This internal arrangement is a classic example of corporate simplification. Before the deal, the ownership structure involved multiple layers: Vodafone held a direct stake in Vodafone Kenya Limited, which in turn held shares in Safaricom, while Vodacom owned the majority of Vodafone Kenya.

By buying out Vodafone's remaining 12.5% stake in Vodafone Kenya Limited—equivalent to that 5% effective interest in Safaricom—Vodacom gained 100% ownership of the Kenyan holding vehicle. The Sh68 billion was the price of cleaning up that structure, and it went straight to Vodafone.

The Kenyan Government's Sh204 Billion External Payout

The Kenyan government, by contrast, received genuinely external funds. Its Sh204 billion payment from Vodacom for the 15% stake represents real cash entering the state's accounts, which the Treasury indicated would go toward infrastructure development and sovereign wealth funds.

Vodafone's Sh68 billion, however, was an intra-group transfer. Vodafone was both the seller of the 5% interest and, through its control of Vodacom, the ultimate source of the funds used to buy it.

A Neat Accounting Manoeuvre or Sensible Housekeeping?

Critics might describe this as a neat accounting manoeuvre. Supporters would call it sensible corporate housekeeping. Either way, the outcome is that Vodafone and Vodacom now fully consolidate Safaricom, gaining controlling ownership of a business with over 38 million M-Pesa customers and a market capitalisation of roughly €7.7 billion.

Vodafone's CEO, Margherita Della Valle, framed the move as a growth opportunity in an attractive market, noting the long partnership since 2000 that produced M-Pesa.

What This Means for Safaricom's NSE Listing

For Safaricom itself, the ownership change means little on the surface. The company remains listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, with the following shareholding structure:

  • Vodacom: 55%
  • Kenyan government: 20%
  • Public investors: 25%

But beneath the surface, the deal reveals how large multinationals can rearrange their African assets with minimal external cash outflow. Vodafone did not need to find a buyer for its Safaricom slice; it simply directed its own subsidiary to buy it, using funds that ultimately belonged to the group anyway. The Sh68 billion never left the family.
